newsitem.title: JAPAN: East Asian buyers eye Australian feed wheat plans.
newsitem.headline: East Asian buyers eye Australian feed wheat plans.

text.p: East Asian animal feed importers said on Monday they would monitor Australia's proposal to develop a winter longseason feed wheat crop aimed at the Asian market, but were mixed in their reaction as potential buyers.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), which developed the new variety after decades of effort, said last week it sees the prospect of a 3.0-4.0 million tonne crop in four to five years.
The first commercial production of Australian red winter wheat is taking place in the current 1996/97 season at the trial level of 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes.
Japan's Food Agency and traders said they would buy the Australian feed wheat if the crop proves price competitive against other origins and feeds, in particular U.S. corn.
"We once used Australian wheat as a feed grain, and local feed makers will ask us to buy if it's cheap enough to compete against U.S. corn," a Food Agency official said.
The agency, the grain trading arm of Japan's Agriculture Ministry, is the sole importer of wheat, barley and rice.
Japan imported about 22,000 tonnes of feed wheat from Australia in the fiscal year 1995/96 ending March, according to the agency's data.

"It makes sense to diversify supply sources of feed grains, from the view point of food security. That was a main reason behind our grain mission to Argentina last year," a grain trader at a major trade house said.
Last year Japan was forced to depend heavily on supplies of U.S. corn, following an earlier export ban on Chinese corn, after domestic supplies of the feed grain fell sharply.
Another trader said quality as well as price would be decisive in determing whether Japan would be a buyer of the Australian wheat.
"It is not only a cheaper price, we need to check to see if the Australian feed wheat is of good quality -- for example does it have the right protein level?" one trader said.
A trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF), the country's largest importer of feed grains, said he had not heard about the Australian plans.
He said NLCF had already changed its plans to purchase feed wheat this year due to a lack of offer prices from foreign suppliers and would buy corn instead.
Feed millers and traders in the Philippines said the country was currently unlikely to purchase Australian feed wheat due to high import tariff barriers.

"Wheat is a poor substitute for corn. Besides, under our present rules wheat importations for feeds are slapped with a 50 percent duty," a trader for one of the Philippines largest feed mills told Reuters.
He said the country's wheat imports, of around three million tonnes a year, are largely used for food.
The government imposes a 10 percent tariff on food wheat imports, he added.
Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero said recently he expected the Philippines'corn imports to reach 500,000 tonnes this year.

A major Taiwanese importer said while the country currently buys about two to three shipments of Australian wheat a year, and is expected to import over 100,000 tonnes in 1997, buyers were unlikely to purchase Australian feed wheat.
He said the country's feed makers processing systems were set up to handle corn, which was the preferred animal feed, and they were unlikely to switch to feed wheat.
